part_title: S3 Storage Class Selection, Availability and Resilience

scenes.title: S3 Storage Classes
scenes.visual_overview: This comparison helps choose storage by frequency, resilience and retrieval deadline.
visual_walkthrough: Seven storage class cards from Standard and IA to Glacier variants
Horizontal spectrum showing less frequent access and longer restores
Intelligent-Tiering automatic and optional archive tiers
Bottom lifecycle diagram: active training data moves from Standard to IA and archive
Exam cue matches latency, AZ resilience and cost
scenes.visual_example: An ML training dataset starts in S3 Standard, then older files transition using configured Lifecycle age rules, eventually to Glacier Flexible or Deep Archive.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Storage class choice is a multidimensional decision, not simply choosing the cheapest gigabyte.
scenes.narration: This slide introduces the seven main S3 storage classes as choices for different access patterns. The overall question is how quickly you need the data, how many Availability Zones should protect it, and what you will pay. Follow the large horizontal spectrum. On the left, S3 Standard supports frequent access and millisecond reads across multiple zones. Standard-IA keeps millisecond access for less frequently read objects; One Zone-IA does the same but places data in one zone, so avoid it for your only irreplaceable copy. The Intelligent-Tiering card monitors changing access and moves eligible objects across automatic tiers, with optional slower archive tiers when configured. Continue into the gold Glacier cards: Instant Retrieval is still millisecond access, Flexible Retrieval requires a restore taking minutes to hours, and Deep Archive prioritizes long retention over immediate reads. The lower example illustrates an AI dataset: keep actively used training files in Standard; use S3 Lifecycle age or date rules to transition older data to IA or eventually archive. Lifecycle follows configured rules, while Intelligent-Tiering reacts to access patterns. The exam cue reminds you that low storage cost may involve retrieval fees, waiting and minimum duration charges. Pick the storage class from the complete requirement, not just the word archive.

scenes.title: S3 Durability and Availability
scenes.visual_overview: This diagram separates preserving object data from being able to access it and compares AZ resilience.
visual_walkthrough: Blue durability shield and gold availability clock definitions
S3 Standard, Standard-IA and Glacier multi-AZ diagrams
One Zone-IA single-AZ diagram and loss risk
Lower backup use case chooses Standard-IA for infrequent but immediate reads
Exam cue distinguishes durability, availability and AZ design
scenes.visual_example: Backup files accessed several times a year must be read in milliseconds and remain resilient across AZs; the pictured choice is Standard-IA.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Eleven nines of designed durability cannot be substituted for an availability promise or for AZ resilience.
scenes.narration: The central lesson here is that durability and availability describe different risks. The blue shield on the left means the data is preserved over time despite failures. The gold clock on the right asks whether an application can read and write that data when it needs to. Follow the storage cards below. S3 Standard and Standard-IA show the bucket protected across multiple Availability Zones. The Glacier card also represents durable multi-zone archival storage. One Zone-IA is deliberately drawn with only one AZ: it is lower cost for data you can recreate, but loss of that zone can mean losing the object. The slide is comparing resilience and access, not suggesting all classes have identical availability. Now follow its worked example at the bottom. A business has backup files that are rarely accessed, wants lower storage cost, and still needs immediate reads and multi-AZ protection. The arrow leads to S3 Standard-IA rather than One Zone-IA or a slow archive class. That example teaches a useful decision method: establish whether losing one AZ is acceptable, then establish the maximum retrieval delay. Durability is resistance to data loss; availability is timely access. Neither is a guarantee that a restore or recovery plan will succeed without testing.

scenes.title: S3 Standard: General Purpose
scenes.visual_overview: How frequent, low-latency machine-learning access maps to S3 Standard rather than infrequent or archival classes.
visual_walkthrough: Left S3 Standard bucket with frequent access, low latency and multi-AZ resilience
Three arrows to frequent consistent usage, real-time reads and AZ protection
Right comparisons with Standard-IA and three Glacier retrieval types
Bottom training data flows from S3 Standard to SageMaker
Exam cue chooses class by access pattern
scenes.visual_example: An actively trained SageMaker model frequently reads input images, documents and data from an S3 Standard bucket.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Use Standard when repeated immediate access and multi-zone resilience matter, rather than treating archival price as the sole decision.
scenes.narration: This visual focuses on the general-purpose S3 Standard class. Its main message is that actively used AI data needs reliably fast reads, not just cheap long-term storage. Read the large left panel first: frequent access, low-latency retrieval, and resilience across multiple Availability Zones are the three characteristics. The arrows lead to the matching decisions in the middle: consistent access, real-time or low-latency reads, and a need for multi-zone protection. Now examine the two comparison boxes on the right. Standard-IA also offers millisecond reads but has retrieval charges and a minimum duration charge, making it better when reads are uncommon. The Glacier options differ again: Glacier Instant Retrieval offers immediate reads for rarely used archival objects, while Flexible and Deep Archive need a restore before data is used. The lower example ties the choice to a real ML workflow. Training images, documents and other input data enter S3 Standard and SageMaker reads them repeatedly while training a model. Choosing an archive class just because it is cheaper per gigabyte can delay training and create avoidable retrieval cost. The entire picture teaches that matching the storage class to workload behavior is more important than ranking classes from expensive to cheap.
